questions.question: A large enterprise needs to enforce that all Azure resources must be deployed only in specific regions (West Europe and North Europe) across 80 subscriptions. New subscriptions added in the future must automatically comply. What is the MOST scalable approach?
options: Create a custom RBAC role in each subscription that restricts deployment to those regions
Use Azure Blueprints to deploy resource locks in each subscription denying deployments outside the target regions
Enable Azure Defender and configure geo-restriction alerts for deployments in non-approved regions
Configure Azure Policy 'Allowed locations' initiative at the Management Group level and assign it to the root management group.
questions.explanation: Azure Policy assigned at a Management Group scope applies to ALL subscriptions within that group hierarchy, including subscriptions added in the future. The built-in 'Allowed locations' policy definition (or an initiative containing it) enforces the region constraint at creation time with a Deny effect. RBAC cannot restrict deployment regions. Blueprints are a deployment mechanism, not a continuous enforcement control. Azure Defender is a threat detection service. it automatically applies to all current and future subscriptions underneath

questions.question: A solutions architect must design an identity solution for a company with 10,000 on-premises Active Directory users who need SSO access to Azure resources and Microsoft 365. The company cannot allow password hashes to be stored in the cloud for compliance reasons. Which hybrid identity method satisfies this requirement?
options: Password Hash Synchronization (PHS) — sync password hashes to Azure AD for cloud authentication
Pass-Through Authentication (PTA).
Azure AD Connect with ADFS federation — authentication happens on-premises via ADFS; Azure AD acts as relying party
Azure AD B2C with custom policies to integrate on-premises directory
questions.explanation: Pass-Through Authentication (PTA) validates users' passwords directly against on-premises Active Directory. No password hashes or tokens are stored in Azure AD — the authentication agent on-premises handles validation and returns a success/fail response. This satisfies compliance requirements that prohibit cloud storage of password hashes. ADFS federation also works but requires significant on-premises infrastructure. PHS explicitly stores password hashes in Azure AD, violating the requirement. authentication requests pass through to on-premises AD; no password hashes stored in cloud

questions.question: An architect needs to grant a team of junior developers access to create and manage resources within a specific resource group, but prevent them from modifying any IAM/RBAC assignments. Which RBAC role combination achieves least-privilege?
options: Assign the Owner role at the resource group scope to give full management capability
Assign the Reader role plus a custom role with write permissions on specific resource types
Assign the Contributor role at the resource group scope.
Assign the User Access Administrator role scoped to the resource group
questions.explanation: The built-in Contributor role provides full rights to create, delete, and manage resources but explicitly does NOT include Microsoft.Authorization/* actions (assigning/removing roles, creating policy assignments). This is the correct least-privilege choice: full resource management without IAM modification rights. Owner includes Microsoft.Authorization/* which allows granting access. User Access Administrator is specifically for managing role assignments, the opposite of what's needed. Contributor allows resource management but explicitly excludes the ability to grant access to others (no Microsoft.Authorization/* actions)

questions.question: A company's operations team needs to collect OS-level performance metrics (custom memory counters, application logs) from 500 Azure VMs and on-premises servers into a central workspace for dashboards and alerts. Which Azure Monitor component collects this data?
options: Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) installed on VMs,.
Application Insights SDK integrated into the operating system for infrastructure telemetry
Azure Monitor Diagnostic Settings — routes platform logs to Log Analytics without agent installation
Azure Monitor Metrics — collects platform-level metrics from Azure resources without agents
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) is the modern unified agent replacing the legacy Log Analytics Agent (MMA) and Diagnostics Agent. It uses Data Collection Rules (DCRs) to define which data sources to collect (Windows Event Logs, Syslog, performance counters, custom text logs) and which workspace(s) to send data to. AMA works on Azure VMs, on-premises servers, and multi-cloud VMs. Platform metrics don't require an agent but cannot collect OS-level custom counters. configured with Data Collection Rules (DCRs) to send to a Log Analytics workspace

questions.question: An architect is designing a resource management strategy for a large organization with 3 business units, each with Dev/Test/Prod environments. They need separate billing, access isolation, and policy enforcement per environment. What structure best reflects this?
options: One subscription for all environments with resource groups per business unit and environment
An Azure Tenant per business unit with cross-tenant subscriptions for shared services
One subscription per environment type (Dev subscription, Test subscription, Prod subscription) for all business units
A management group hierarchy: Root → Business Unit MGs → Environment MGs.
questions.explanation: AZ-305 best practice for enterprise-scale: Management Groups provide policy/RBAC inheritance hierarchy. Separate subscriptions per BU×Environment provide billing isolation (each subscription has its own cost view), resource quota isolation, and a strong blast radius boundary. Policies assigned at the Environment MG (e.g., no public IPs in Prod) cascade to all BU Prod subscriptions automatically. One subscription for all environments creates governance and billing challenges. Multiple tenants add identity complexity without proportional benefit. with one subscription per business unit × environment combination (9 subscriptions total), policies and RBAC assigned at MG level

questions.question: A company needs to provide developers with self-service access to pre-approved Azure environments (specific VM sizes, approved images, region restrictions) without granting them broad subscription permissions. Which Azure service supports this governance pattern?
options: Azure Managed Applications to publish approved resource configurations to an internal service catalog,.
Azure Policy with allowed SKU definitions and approved image lists
Azure Blueprints to deploy pre-approved environments as reusable packages
Azure Resource Manager templates deployed by a central ops team on-demand
questions.explanation: Azure Managed Applications published to a Service Catalog allow operators to define pre-approved resource packages (VMs with specific SKUs, approved OS images, networking configurations) that developers can deploy from the Azure portal without seeing the underlying ARM templates or having broad RBAC permissions. The managed resource group is owned by the publisher, ensuring approved configurations. Blueprints are for subscription-level governance scaffolding, not per-developer self-service deployments. allowing developers to deploy from a curated marketplace

questions.question: An architect needs to design a solution where no single person can approve their own access to sensitive resources. All privileged role activations must require approval from a second person and generate an audit log. Which Azure feature provides this?
options: Azure AD Access Reviews running monthly to detect unauthorized role assignments
Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM) with eligible role assignments and approval workflows requiring a designated approver before activation
Azure RBAC with deny assignments to block self-approval
Azure AD Conditional Access with role assignment conditions
questions.explanation: PIM eligible assignments require users to activate the role (not permanently assigned) and can be configured to require multi-person approval before activation. The approver receives a notification, reviews the business justification, and approves or denies. All activation requests, approvals, and denials are logged in Azure AD audit logs. Access Reviews verify existing assignments but don't enforce real-time approval workflows for new activations.

questions.question: A company wants to receive proactive alerts when their Azure costs exceed $10,000 in a given month, and automatically suspend non-critical development VMs when spending reaches 90% of the budget. Which Azure feature enables both of these?
options: Azure Monitor metric alerts on billing metrics with Logic App workflows for VM management
Azure Advisor cost recommendations with automated remediation enabled
Azure Cost Management + Billing budget with action groups: email alert at 80%, runbook automation at 90%
Azure Policy with cost-based deny effects that prevent new resource creation above budget
questions.explanation: Azure Cost Management budgets allow you to set monthly spending thresholds with alert thresholds at multiple percentages (e.g., 80% and 90% of budget). At 90%, an action group can trigger an Azure Automation Runbook or Logic App that stops the development VMs. Email alerts notify cost owners at any threshold. Azure Advisor provides recommendations but not automated enforcement. Azure Policy cannot enforce budget-based restrictions.

questions.question: A solutions architect must ensure that all resource groups in a production subscription have specific tags (CostCenter, Owner, Environment) applied at the time of creation. Resources without these tags must not be created. Which Azure Policy effect enforces this?
options: Audit — logs non-compliant resources to the compliance dashboard
Modify — adds missing tags automatically but still allows creation with remediation tasks
Append — automatically adds missing tags with default values without blocking creation
Deny — rejects the deployment if required tags are missing
questions.explanation: The Deny policy effect is evaluated at request time and rejects the deployment if the conditions are met (required tags missing). Audit logs non-compliance but doesn't prevent it. Append adds fields to requests (e.g., can add tags if not provided, but cannot enforce specific non-empty values). Modify is used with remediation tasks to update existing resources but doesn't block new deployments. For mandatory tag enforcement at creation time, Deny is the correct effect.

questions.question: An architect needs to design a solution to prevent accidental deletion of a critical Azure SQL Database. Even subscription owners should not be able to delete it without explicit action. Which control achieves this?
options: Apply a CanNotDelete resource lock to the Azure SQL Database.
Assign a custom RBAC role denying Microsoft.Sql/servers/databases/delete to all users
Enable Azure Backup for the database with immutable vault settings
Apply a ReadOnly resource lock to the Azure SQL Database — it prevents all modifications including deletion
questions.explanation: Resource locks override RBAC — even subscription Owners cannot perform the locked action without first removing the lock. CanNotDelete allows read and modify operations but blocks delete. ReadOnly blocks ALL writes including beneficial operations like scaling, failover, and configuration changes — too restrictive for a production database. RBAC deny assignments could work but cannot block subscription Owners who have the ability to modify RBAC. Backup provides recovery but doesn't prevent deletion. it prevents deletion but allows modifications

questions.question: A solutions architect is designing a monitoring strategy. The application team needs to detect performance regressions in a .NET web application running on Azure App Service, including dependency call durations, exception rates, and user session tracking. Which monitoring solution is most appropriate?
options: Azure Network Watcher for packet capture and latency analysis of incoming requests
Azure Monitor Metrics for App Service — tracks CPU, memory, requests per second
Application Insights connected to the App Service.
Log Analytics workspace with custom log queries on IIS access logs
questions.explanation: Application Insights is the Azure APM (Application Performance Monitoring) service purpose-built for application-level telemetry. It captures: HTTP request/response telemetry, dependency call durations (SQL, HTTP, Service Bus), exceptions and stack traces, custom events/metrics, user sessions (via JavaScript SDK), and availability tests. It integrates with distributed tracing (correlation IDs across microservices). Platform metrics only cover infrastructure. Log Analytics requires custom parsing. Network Watcher focuses on network-layer diagnostics. provides request tracing, dependency tracking, exception telemetry, user sessions, and availability monitoring with a distributed tracing model

questions.question: A company has a requirement to store Azure Activity Logs and Azure AD Sign-In Logs for 2 years for compliance purposes. The data must be queryable. Which design achieves this cost-effectively?
options: Configure Diagnostic Settings to route logs to Azure Storage (Archive tier) for long-term cheap retention; for querying.
Configure Diagnostic Settings to route logs to a Log Analytics workspace with a 2-year retention period set
Export logs to Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 and use Azure Synapse Analytics for queries
Enable Microsoft Sentinel with a 2-year data retention policy — Sentinel indexes all logs for querying
questions.explanation: The cost-effective two-tier pattern: Log Analytics for active querying (90-day hot retention, after which logs are archived automatically) with logs also sent to Azure Storage (cool/archive tier) for compliance retention at low cost (~$0.002/GB/month for archive vs ~$2-3/GB/month for Log Analytics ingestion). Log Analytics workspace retention beyond 90 days incurs significant costs. This dual-destination approach via Diagnostic Settings is the AZ-305-recommended pattern for cost-optimized compliance logging. also stream to a Log Analytics workspace with 90-day retention for active analysis

questions.question: An architect is designing a BCDR solution for an on-premises application that must failover to Azure within 4 hours (RTO) and lose no more than 1 hour of data (RPO). The application runs on VMware VMs. Which Azure service meets these requirements?
options: Azure VMware Solution (AVS) with stretched clusters across on-premises and Azure
Azure Migrate to convert VMware VMs to Azure VMs, then configure availability sets
Azure Site Recovery (ASR) replicating VMware VMs to Azure.
Azure Backup for VMware VMs with a 1-hour backup frequency
questions.explanation: Azure Site Recovery provides continuous replication of VMware VMs to Azure with RPO as low as 15 seconds for Hyper-V and 5 minutes for VMware VMs using agentless replication. Automated recovery plans can failover hundreds of VMs in sequence, meeting a 4-hour RTO. Azure Backup provides scheduled snapshots (not continuous replication) and cannot meet 1-hour RPO reliably. Azure Migrate is a one-time migration tool, not a BCDR solution. AVS is a full VMware environment in Azure, overengineered for this requirement. supports RPO as low as 15 minutes and automated failover within minutes

questions.question: A solutions architect needs to design high availability for an Azure SQL Database supporting a mission-critical application with an RTO of less than 30 seconds and an RPO of near-zero. What configuration achieves this?
options: Azure SQL Database with Point-in-Time Restore configured for 1-minute granularity
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale tier with distributed read replicas for zero-RPO reads
Azure SQL Database with Geo-Replication — synchronously replicates to a secondary in another region
Azure SQL Database Business Critical tier with Auto-Failover Groups.
questions.explanation: Business Critical tier uses an Always On availability group with 3-4 replicas in the same region, providing 99.995% SLA (< 26 min downtime/year) and sub-second failover. Auto-Failover Groups extend this to cross-region with configurable failover policies. Active Geo-Replication is ASYNCHRONOUS — it has potential data loss. Point-in-Time Restore is a recovery mechanism, not a HA mechanism (RTO is minutes to hours). Hyperscale read replicas are for scale-out reads, not HA failover. provides synchronous replication within the primary region (Business Critical SLA 99.995%) and automatic failover with data loss < 5 seconds

questions.question: An architect must ensure that Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS) hosting a stateless web application remain available if a single Azure datacenter fails. The application requires minimum 3 healthy instances at all times. How should the VMSS be configured?
options: Deploy two separate VMSS in two different regions and use Azure Traffic Manager for DNS failover
Deploy the VMSS in a single region with an Availability Set and 3 fault domains
Deploy the VMSS across 3 Availability Zones with a zone-redundant load balancer and set minimum instances to 3
Deploy the VMSS with a Premium SSD managed disk for high availability
questions.explanation: Availability Zones are physically separate datacenters within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking. Deploying across 3 AZs means the VMSS survives a complete datacenter failure with instances in the other 2 AZs still serving traffic. The zone-redundant load balancer distributes traffic across all AZs. A minimum of 3 instances means at least 1 per zone. Availability Sets protect against rack/update domain failures within a single datacenter — not datacenter-level failures.

questions.question: A company needs to replicate an Azure SQL Database to a secondary region for disaster recovery. In the event of a regional outage, the failover should happen automatically without manual intervention. Which feature provides automatic cross-region failover?
options: Active Geo-Replication with manual failover using Failover Groups API
Azure Database for PostgreSQL with geo-redundant backups and geo-restore
Auto-Failover Groups — groups one or more databases with automatic failover to the secondary region if the primary becomes unavailable for a configurable grace period
Azure SQL Managed Instance cross-instance failover with Business Critical tier
questions.explanation: Auto-Failover Groups are an abstraction on top of Active Geo-Replication that provide: a read-write listener DNS name (always points to primary), a read-only listener (points to secondary), automatic failover triggered after a configurable grace period (default 1 hour), and automatic DNS update during failover so applications reconnect transparently. Active Geo-Replication requires manual failover. Geo-restore is a backup restore operation (hours RTO). SQL Managed Instance failover groups exist but the question asks about SQL Database.

questions.question: An architect needs to design a backup strategy for 200 Azure VMs across 5 subscriptions, ensuring all VMs are backed up daily with 30-day retention. A central team must be able to monitor backup compliance from a single dashboard. What is the recommended design?
options: Deploy a third-party backup solution from Azure Marketplace that supports multi-subscription management
Create a Recovery Services Vault in each subscription and configure VM backup policies individually
Enable Azure Snapshot Center in Azure Monitor to schedule VM snapshots across subscriptions
Use Azure Backup Center to manage backup policies centrally across all Recovery Services Vaults and subscriptions.
questions.explanation: Azure Backup Center is the unified management portal for all Azure Backup workloads across subscriptions, regions, and vault types. Combined with Azure Policy (built-in 'Configure backup on VMs with a given tag' policy), you can automatically enroll new VMs into backup, enforce retention policies, and monitor compliance status from a single pane. Recovery Services Vaults are still per-region/subscription but managed centrally. Backup Center provides cross-subscription reporting, compliance, and job monitoring dashboards. deploy a single backup policy via Azure Policy to enforce daily backup with 30-day retention on all VMs

questions.question: A company is designing its Azure storage strategy. Large files (video content, 50-500 GB each) will be uploaded once and accessed frequently for the first 30 days, rarely for the next 60 days, then almost never after 90 days. What lifecycle management policy minimizes cost?
options: Store all files in Hot tier, manually move to Cool after 30 days
Store in Premium tier for fast initial access, then delete after 90 days
Use Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 with auto-tiering enabled for large binary objects
Configure a Blob lifecycle policy: transition to Cool tier at 30 days.
questions.explanation: Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management policies automate tier transitions based on last-modified time. The cost tiers (Hot > Cool > Cold > Archive) allow optimizing cost vs access latency. For this pattern: Hot (30 days, frequent access), Cool (30-90 days, infrequent), Archive (90+ days, near-zero access). Archive is the cheapest tier (~$0.00099/GB/month) but has rehydration latency (hours). Lifecycle policies run daily and transition blobs automatically, eliminating manual operations. to Archive tier at 90 days — Archive is the cheapest storage tier at ~$0.002/GB/month

questions.question: A company requires a relational database solution that supports elastic scaling of compute independently of storage, can pause compute when not in use (dev/test scenarios), and provides per-second billing. Which Azure SQL offering fits?
options: Azure SQL Database Serverless compute tier.
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale tier with 0 replicas for dev/test
Azure SQL Managed Instance with serverless compute tier
Azure SQL Database Business Critical tier with auto-scaling groups
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Database Serverless is purpose-built for intermittent, unpredictable usage patterns. It auto-scales compute vCores between a configured min and max based on workload, auto-pauses after a configurable inactivity period (minimum 60 minutes), and auto-resumes when a connection arrives (with a brief cold-start delay). Billing is per-second for active compute, plus per-GB for storage. This makes it ideal for dev/test databases that are idle nights and weekends. Business Critical and Managed Instance don't support auto-pause. auto-pauses after configurable inactivity period, auto-resumes on next connection, bills per second of compute usage

questions.question: An architect needs to choose a NoSQL database for a global e-commerce application that processes 1 million product catalog reads per second with single-digit millisecond latency. The data model is simple key-value lookups on product ID. Which Azure database service is most appropriate?
options: Azure Table Storage — a simple NoSQL key-value store with lower cost than Cosmos DB
Azure Cosmos DB with the NoSQL API.
Azure SQL Database with in-memory OLTP for high-throughput reads
Azure Cache for Redis for temporary product catalog caching with write-through to SQL
questions.explanation: Azure Cosmos DB is designed for planet-scale NoSQL with: single-digit millisecond read/write latency at the 99th percentile, automatic multi-region distribution with configurable consistency levels, elastic throughput scaling (Request Units, auto-scale), and 99.999% SLA for multi-region deployments. For 1M reads/second globally, Cosmos DB handles this natively. Azure Table Storage shares the Cosmos DB Table API but has lower SLAs and feature constraints. Redis is an in-memory cache (not a primary database). SQL with in-memory OLTP is still relational and has scaling limits. multi-region distribution, and Bounded Staleness consistency — globally distributed with guaranteed single-digit ms reads at any scale

questions.question: A retail company needs to ingest 50,000 IoT device events per second from sensors, transform the data, and load it into Azure Synapse Analytics for business intelligence reporting every 15 minutes. Which data pipeline architecture is appropriate?
options: Azure IoT Hub → Azure Stream Analytics (real-time transformation) → Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 → Azure Synapse Analytics pipelines for BI ingestion
Azure Event Hubs → Azure Functions (event-by-event processing) → Cosmos DB → Azure Synapse Link for BI
Azure Event Grid → Azure Blob Storage → Azure Data Factory for periodic batch loading to Synapse
Azure IoT Hub → Logic Apps for transformation → Azure SQL Database → Power BI Direct Query
questions.explanation: The standard IoT analytics pattern on Azure: IoT Hub ingests device telemetry at scale (supports millions of devices), Stream Analytics provides real-time SQL-like transformations and windowing functions, ADLS Gen2 acts as the data lake landing zone, and Synapse Analytics pipelines (or Synapse Link) enable BI workloads. Stream Analytics supports 50K events/second and outputs to ADLS with time-based tumbling windows (15 min = perfect match). Logic Apps are for orchestration, not high-throughput stream processing. Event Grid is for event routing, not stream processing.

questions.question: A company wants to run batch machine learning training jobs that require thousands of CPU cores for 4-hour windows, twice a week. After the jobs complete, no compute should be running. What Azure compute solution minimizes cost?
options: Azure Machine Learning compute clusters with min nodes = 0, max nodes = desired scale
Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets with scheduled autoscaling to 0 outside job windows
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) with cluster autoscaler scaling to thousands of nodes
Azure Batch — a managed HPC service that provisions and de-provisions pools of VMs automatically for batch workloads,.
questions.explanation: Azure Batch is specifically designed for large-scale parallel and HPC batch workloads. It manages pools of VMs, job scheduling, task distribution, and automatic scale-to-zero when idle. You only pay for VMs while they're running the batch job. Batch supports spot/low-priority VMs (60-90% discount) for further cost reduction. AML compute clusters also work but add ML-specific overhead. VMSS with scheduled scaling requires management. AKS adds Kubernetes overhead inappropriate for simple HPC batch workloads. supporting massive parallelism with automatic scale-to-zero

questions.question: An architect needs to host a containerized microservices application with 20 services. Some services need to scale to hundreds of instances under load, while others run 1-2 instances constantly. The team wants minimal Kubernetes management overhead. What is the recommended compute platform?
options: Azure Container Instances (ACI) for all 20 services — serverless containers with per-second billing
Azure Functions consumption plan for all 20 microservices — scales to zero when idle
Azure App Service Premium for all services — built-in autoscaling and zero Kubernetes knowledge needed
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS).
questions.explanation: AKS is the recommended platform for containerized microservices requiring mixed scaling patterns. AKS manages the Kubernetes control plane (Azure pays for masters), leaving only node pool management. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling) enables scale-to-zero for idle services. The cluster autoscaler handles node-level scaling. Services needing hundreds of instances use Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) with appropriate resource requests. ACI is for simple on-demand containers, not long-running microservices. App Service doesn't support container orchestration at this complexity. managed Kubernetes control plane, flexible autoscaling with HPA and KEDA, supports both patterns

questions.question: A company is migrating a monolithic .NET Framework 4.8 application to Azure. The application cannot be refactored and requires full IIS control, custom GAC assemblies, and Windows Registry access. Which compute option is appropriate?
options: Azure Container Instances with a Windows container image
Azure App Service (Windows) — managed PaaS with IIS, no VM management, limited deep OS access
Azure Virtual Machines running Windows Server.
Azure Functions with .NET Framework support for serverless refactoring
questions.explanation: When an application requires deep OS-level customization (Windows Registry, GAC, specific IIS module configuration, COM+ components), a Virtual Machine (IaaS) is the appropriate lift-and-shift target. Azure App Service has Windows IIS support but restricts Registry and GAC access. Azure Functions requires refactoring to serverless. Windows containers support GAC but not all Registry paths and COM+ scenarios. The AZ-305 approach: migrate first to IaaS (full compatibility), then modernize to PaaS progressively if feasible. provides full OS control, IIS configuration, GAC, and Registry access for legacy lift-and-shift

questions.question: An architect must design a network topology for Azure where all traffic between spoke VNets must flow through a central hub that contains shared security appliances (next-gen firewall, IDS/IPS). New spoke VNets should connect with minimal configuration. What network topology achieves this?
options: Hub-and-spoke VNet peering with User Defined Routes (UDRs) forcing all inter-spoke traffic through the hub's Network Virtual Appliance (NVA)
Azure Virtual WAN (vWAN) with a Secured Virtual Hub.
Site-to-site VPN connecting each spoke VNet to the hub VNet through VPN Gateway
Full mesh VNet peering between all VNets for direct connectivity
questions.explanation: Azure Virtual WAN Secured Virtual Hub integrates Azure Firewall (or third-party NVAs via NVA infrastructure) directly into the hub and uses intent-based routing to automatically route all inter-spoke and branch traffic through the firewall. New spokes connect to the vWAN hub with minimal configuration and inherit routing automatically. Classic hub-and-spoke with UDRs works but requires manual UDR management on every spoke as new spokes are added. Full mesh doesn't route through a central security point. VPN for VNet-to-VNet adds unnecessary complexity. which includes Azure Firewall or third-party NVA natively and automatically programs routing for all connected spokes

questions.question: A solutions architect must design connectivity from an on-premises datacenter to Azure with guaranteed bandwidth, low latency, and consistent throughput for a financial services application transferring large data sets. Which connectivity option is most appropriate?
options: Site-to-site VPN over the internet — cost-effective with AES-256 encryption
Azure Virtual WAN with point-to-site VPN for all on-premises users
Azure ExpressRoute Direct with Global Reach for direct datacenter-to-datacenter connectivity
Azure ExpressRoute with a dedicated private connection through a network service provider.
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute provides a private, dedicated connection from on-premises to Azure via a connectivity provider, avoiding the public internet entirely. It offers: SLA-backed bandwidth from 50 Mbps to 10 Gbps (100 Gbps with ExpressRoute Direct), consistent latency, and private peering to Azure VNets. Financial services applications with large data transfers need deterministic throughput — internet-based VPN has variable latency and bandwidth. ExpressRoute Direct (option D) is for organizations requiring 100 Gbps direct connectivity, which is over-specified here. provides SLA-backed bandwidth (up to 100 Gbps), predictable latency, and does not traverse the internet

questions.question: A global e-commerce company needs to route user traffic to the nearest Azure region to minimize latency. The solution must also perform health checks and automatically route around a failed region. Which Azure service provides this?
options: Azure Application Gateway with multi-region backend pools
Azure Traffic Manager — DNS-based global traffic routing with configurable routing methods (Performance,.
Azure Front Door — global application delivery platform with anycast routing, WAF, and CDN capabilities
Azure Load Balancer (Standard) with health probes configured across regions
questions.explanation: Azure Traffic Manager is a DNS-based global traffic manager. With the Performance routing method, it directs users to the endpoint with the lowest latency (measured from Azure's distributed monitoring infrastructure). Health probes automatically remove failed endpoints from DNS responses within the configured TTL. Azure Front Door is also valid for global routing with lower latency (anycast, TCP connection reuse), but Traffic Manager is the classic answer for multi-region DNS-level load balancing. The AZ-305 exam specifically tests Traffic Manager routing methods. Geographic, Weighted) and endpoint health monitoring with automatic failover

questions.question: A company has deployed an Azure Application Gateway with WAF for their web application. The security team wants to terminate TLS at the Application Gateway and encrypt the connection between the gateway and backend web servers (end-to-end SSL). How should this be configured?
options: Enable HTTPS backend settings in the Application Gateway with a trusted root certificate for the backend servers.
Deploy Azure API Management in front of the Application Gateway to handle backend TLS
Use Azure Front Door with end-to-end encryption instead — Application Gateway doesn't support backend HTTPS
Configure HTTP backend settings in the Application Gateway — HTTP connections to backends are automatically encrypted
questions.explanation: Application Gateway supports end-to-end SSL by: (1) terminating the client TLS at the frontend listener with a public certificate, (2) re-encrypting the connection to backend servers using backend HTTPS settings with the backend server's certificate (or trusted root CA). You upload the root certificate of the CA that signed the backend certificate. This ensures the full connection is encrypted even between the gateway and internal backend VMs, satisfying end-to-end encryption requirements. ensuring re-encryption between gateway and backend pools

questions.question: An architect is designing a network security strategy for an Azure environment. The requirement is to block all internet egress traffic from VMs and only allow outbound traffic to specific service endpoints (Azure Storage and Azure SQL). How should this be implemented?
options: Configure Azure Firewall to allow only outbound traffic to Azure Storage and SQL public IPs
Use Private Endpoints for Storage and SQL, then add a UDR pointing all 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to an NVA that blocks internet egress while allowing Private Endpoint traffic
Use NSG outbound rules to deny internet traffic and allow traffic to Storage and SQL service tags;.
Deploy a NAT Gateway and configure route tables to block internet traffic
questions.explanation: NSG outbound rules with service tags allow traffic to 'Storage.EastUS' and 'Sql.EastUS' service tag ranges, then deny all internet traffic (0.0.0.0/0). VNet Service Endpoints for Storage and SQL ensure traffic from the VNet to these services routes through the Azure backbone (not the internet) and the Storage/SQL firewall can restrict access to the specific VNet subnet. This is simpler and cheaper than Azure Firewall for service-specific egress control. Private Endpoints (option D) also work but are more complex and costly. configure VNet Service Endpoints for Storage and SQL so traffic routes through the Azure backbone without internet

questions.question: A company is planning to migrate 200 on-premises servers to Azure. The migration team needs to discover and assess all servers (VMware, physical, Hyper-V) to understand dependencies, right-size VM SKUs in Azure, and estimate monthly costs before migrating. Which Azure service provides this assessment capability?
options: Azure Site Recovery with pre-migration assessment reports
Azure Monitor with Dependency Map to discover server relationships
Azure Migrate with the Discovery and Assessment tool.
Azure Cost Management + Billing with right-sizing recommendations via Azure Advisor
questions.explanation: Azure Migrate is the centralized hub for Azure migration. The Discovery and Assessment project: deploys a lightweight appliance (on-premises VM) that discovers VMware, Hyper-V, or physical servers without requiring agents for basic discovery. It provides: right-sized Azure VM SKU recommendations based on actual performance data, dependency mapping (with Dependency Agent for detailed maps), monthly cost estimates for compute and storage, and readiness assessment for Azure. ASR is a migration/replication tool, not an assessment tool. uses lightweight appliances to discover VMware/Hyper-V/physical servers, maps dependencies via agentless or agent-based dependency analysis, provides Azure SKU right-sizing recommendations and monthly cost estimates

questions.question: An architect needs to migrate a 10 TB on-premises SQL Server database to Azure SQL Managed Instance with minimal downtime. The migration must not impact production during business hours. Which service and approach achieves this?
options: Detach the database MDF/LDF files, upload to Azure Blob Storage, attach to SQL MI
Use SQL Server Replication to replicate all databases to SQL Managed Instance, then switch application connection strings
Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) in online migration mode.
Azure Backup for SQL Server, restore to SQL Managed Instance
questions.explanation: Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) in online mode provides continuous data replication: the initial full load is followed by continuous incremental sync of transaction log changes. Production writes to the source SQL Server during the migration, and DMS keeps the target SQL MI synchronized. When ready to cut over, you stop applications briefly, let DMS sync the final changes, then switch connection strings. This minimizes downtime to just the final cutover window (typically minutes). Backup/restore and file attach are offline migration methods requiring full downtime. continuously syncs changes from on-premises SQL Server to SQL MI after initial load, allowing cutover during a low-activity maintenance window with minimal downtime

questions.question: A company needs to move 500 TB of data from on-premises NAS to Azure Blob Storage. The internet connection is only 100 Mbps and encrypting 500 TB over the internet would take 46+ days. Which Azure data transfer service eliminates this constraint?
options: Azure Data Factory with parallel self-hosted integration runtime for accelerated transfer
Azure Import/Export service — send physical hard drives to an Azure datacenter for direct import
Azure ExpressRoute with 10 Gbps circuit for bulk data transfer
Azure Data Box — a physical appliance shipped to the customer.
questions.explanation: Azure Data Box is Microsoft's offline data transfer solution for large datasets. The Data Box holds 80 TB usable (100 TB raw) per unit, uses AES-256 encryption, and can be ordered in quantities. For 500 TB, use Data Box Heavy (770 TB usable) or multiple Data Box units. The physical device ships to your datacenter, you load data locally at network/disk speed (bypassing internet bandwidth), then ship it back to Azure. Microsoft uploads the data and sends you a certificate of data erasure. ExpressRoute requires 2-3 months procurement. Data Factory requires available bandwidth. loaded with up to 80 TB (or 100 TB Disk), shipped back to Azure where data is uploaded to Azure Storage securely

questions.question: An e-commerce application experiences Black Friday spikes of 100x normal traffic. The application is hosted on Azure App Service. The architect wants the application to scale out automatically based on HTTP request queue length, not just CPU. Which autoscaling approach enables custom metric scaling?
options: Azure App Service automatic scaling (preview) based on HTTP latency metrics
Configure App Service autoscale rules based on the 'HttpQueueLength' metric from the App Service Plan.
Use Azure Traffic Manager to distribute traffic across multiple App Service plans when load increases
Deploy Azure Front Door with origin groups to handle traffic spikes at the CDN layer before reaching App Service
questions.explanation: Azure App Service exposes custom metrics including HttpQueueLength (number of requests waiting in the HTTP queue) that can trigger autoscale rules. This metric is more relevant for queue-based bottlenecks than CPU — a healthy app might have low CPU but a growing HTTP queue if I/O-bound. Autoscale rules: scale out when HttpQueueLength > 10 (add instances), scale in when < 1 (remove instances). This provides more responsive scaling than CPU for web workloads. Traffic Manager is DNS-level, not application-level autoscaling. scale out when queue length > 10, scale in when < 1

questions.question: A solutions architect needs to design an API layer for a microservices application. The API must support rate limiting, request/response transformation, authentication (JWT validation), developer portal for API documentation, and monetization through subscription keys. Which Azure service provides all of these capabilities?
options: Azure API Management (APIM).
Azure Application Gateway with WAF for API security and routing
Azure Functions with custom middleware for all cross-cutting concerns
Azure Front Door with custom rules engine for API routing and security
questions.explanation: Azure API Management is specifically designed as a full-lifecycle API management platform. Key features: Inbound/outbound policies (rate limiting, IP filtering, JWT validation, header transformation), OAuth2/OpenID Connect integration, developer portal (auto-generated API documentation, subscription management), product tiers with subscription keys for monetization, built-in analytics, and backend load balancing. Application Gateway and Front Door are network-layer load balancers without API management capabilities. Azure Functions require building all cross-cutting concerns from scratch. provides a full API gateway with policies for rate limiting, transformation, JWT validation, OAuth2, developer portal, product subscriptions, and analytics

questions.question: An architect is designing a solution for an application that processes financial transactions. Each transaction must be processed exactly once, in order, and failures must be retried without duplicate processing. Which messaging pattern is most appropriate?
options: Azure Event Hubs for real-time transaction streaming with consumer groups
Azure Storage Queue with at-least-once delivery and application-level deduplication logic
Azure Service Bus Queues with message sessions enabled for ordered delivery.
Azure Event Grid for event-driven transaction processing with retry policies
questions.explanation: Service Bus Queues provide exactly-once, ordered processing through: (1) Message Sessions — enables FIFO ordering per session key (e.g., account ID), ensuring transactions for the same account are processed in order, (2) Duplicate detection — if a message is resent with the same MessageId within a configurable window, Service Bus discards the duplicate, (3) Dead-letter queue (DLQ) for messages that fail after max retries. Event Hubs is optimized for high-throughput telemetry streaming, not reliable ordered business transactions. Storage Queue has no ordering guarantee and no duplicate detection. dead-letter queue for failures, and duplicate detection enabled

questions.question: A developer team wants to deploy a web application using containers to Azure with no Kubernetes management overhead, automatic HTTPS, built-in scale-to-zero, and support for sidecar containers. Which Azure service provides all of these?
options: Azure Container Apps — fully managed container environment built on Kubernetes (KEDA + Dapr).
Azure Container Instances (ACI) — serverless containers with no cluster management
Azure App Service with Docker container deployment
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) with a serverless node pool using Virtual Nodes
questions.explanation: Azure Container Apps is the modern PaaS for microservices containers without Kubernetes management. It provides: KEDA-based autoscaling including scale-to-zero, built-in HTTPS ingress with auto-managed TLS certificates, sidecar container support (Dapr integration), revision management for blue-green deployments, and support for event-driven architectures. ACI is for single containers without built-in HTTP ingress or KEDA scaling. App Service supports containers but doesn't support sidecars natively. AKS requires cluster management. supporting autoscaling including scale-to-zero, HTTPS ingress, and sidecar containers without Kubernetes management

questions.question: A company processes 10 million Azure AD sign-in logs per day and needs to retain them for 90 days with the ability to query specific user sign-in events interactively. Log Analytics ingestion costs are a concern. Which cost-optimized design supports this?
options: Ingest all 10M daily logs to a Log Analytics workspace — standard ingestion pricing applies to all logs
Use Microsoft Sentinel with Log Analytics workspace in a commitment tier for volume pricing discount
Archive logs to Azure Storage and query with a self-hosted ELK stack
Use Diagnostic Settings to send Azure AD Sign-In Logs to a Log Analytics workspace with the Basic plan logs table (ingested at lower cost but with limited retention and query capabilities)
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor Logs introduced Basic and Auxiliary log plans (alongside the standard Analytics plan). Basic plan: significantly lower ingestion cost (~$0.50/GB vs ~$2.30/GB for Analytics), 8-day interactive query retention, archival for up to 12 years. For Azure AD Sign-In Logs where you primarily need to search specific events (not complex analytics), the Basic plan delivers significant cost savings. Analytics plan provides full KQL capabilities but at higher cost. The AZ-305 cost optimization domain tests knowledge of log plan tiers.

questions.question: An organization must implement multi-region active-active deployment for a web application with shared state. Users must always be routed to the nearest healthy region, and sessions must be consistent across regions. Which Azure services form this architecture?
options: Azure Traffic Manager with Geographic routing; Azure SQL Database with Active Geo-Replication for read-only replicas in each region
Azure Front Door for global traffic routing with origin health probes;.
Azure Load Balancer Standard (cross-region preview) with Azure Cache for Redis geo-replication
Azure Application Gateway in each region with Traffic Manager DNS; Azure SQL Database with Auto-Failover Groups for session data
questions.explanation: Azure Front Door provides global anycast routing to the nearest healthy region with sub-second health probe detection and automatic failover. For active-active with shared session state, Cosmos DB with multi-region write (also called multi-master) is the key: any region can write sessions, with automatic conflict resolution and replication to all regions. SQL Geo-Replication (option B) provides read-only secondaries — cannot write to secondaries in active-active. Redis geo-replication is asynchronous and doesn't support multi-master writes. Azure Cosmos DB with multi-region write enabled for consistent session state across regions

questions.question: A company's security team requires that all access to Azure Key Vault secrets from application VMs happens over private network paths — no public internet. The VMs are in an Azure VNet. Which network design achieves this?
options: Enable Key Vault firewall and add the VNet subnet to the allowed Virtual Networks list using Service Endpoints
Deploy Azure Firewall and add Key Vault FQDN to allowed application rules
Configure NSG rules to block all outbound traffic except to Key Vault public IPs
Deploy a Private Endpoint for the Key Vault in the application VNet.
questions.explanation: Private Endpoints create a private network interface with a private IP address within your VNet for the Key Vault. Azure Private DNS Zones override public DNS resolution so 'vault.vault.azure.net' resolves to the private IP instead of the public endpoint. All traffic from VMs to Key Vault flows through the VNet/backbone, never traversing the internet. Service Endpoints (option A) keep traffic on the backbone but the Key Vault endpoint is still a public IP from the VM's perspective — it doesn't provide full private connectivity for all scenarios. Private Endpoint is the recommended approach for strict private access requirements. the vault gets a private IP within the VNet, DNS resolves to the private IP, all traffic stays within Azure backbone

questions.question: A startup is designing its first Azure application — a web app with a REST API backend and a SQL database. The team has 2 developers and needs to be productive with minimal infrastructure management. The expected load is 100-500 users/day for the first 6 months. What is the most appropriate architecture?
options: Azure App Service (Free or Basic tier) for the web app and API.
Azure Kubernetes Service with managed node pools, Ingress controller, Azure SQL Database
Azure Virtual Machines for API (Windows Server + IIS), Azure SQL Database Basic tier, Azure Application Gateway
Azure Functions consumption plan for the API, Cosmos DB serverless for data, Static Web Apps for frontend
questions.explanation: For a small team with minimal operations overhead and low initial load, PaaS services are ideal: App Service manages OS patching, scaling, and TLS; Azure SQL Database manages backup, patching, and HA. The Basic/Standard DTU tiers are cost-effective for 100-500 users/day. Application Insights provides out-of-the-box APM. This is the AZ-305 principle of 'right-sizing and right-tiering' — AKS is over-engineered for a 2-person startup. VMs add infrastructure management burden. Functions/Cosmos DB works but adds complexity when the team may not need it yet. Azure SQL Database (DTU-based S0 or S1 tier), Azure Application Insights for monitoring — managed PaaS services with zero infrastructure management

questions.question: An architect needs to design an Azure AD identity solution that allows external business partners to sign in using their own organizational credentials (Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, or SAML IdP) to access a shared portal. Partner users should not have accounts created in the host directory. Which feature enables this?
options: Azure AD Connect to sync partner AD forests into the host directory
Azure AD B2C with custom user flows for partner onboarding
Azure AD External Identities B2B collaboration.
Azure AD Domain Services to provide Kerberos authentication for partner accounts
questions.explanation: Azure AD External Identities (B2B) allows external partners to use their existing credentials (Entra ID, Google, SAML/WS-Fed IdP, or Microsoft Account) to access shared applications. A lightweight guest object is created in the host directory representing the external identity, but the partner's password is never stored — authentication happens at the partner's IdP. The host admin can control access via Conditional Access, Entitlement Management, and Access Reviews. B2C is designed for consumer-facing apps where users create accounts. AD Connect syncs accounts, which would create full member accounts. partners sign in using their own identity provider credentials, Azure AD issues a guest account linked to their external identity without storing credentials

questions.question: A company needs to enforce a standard set of Azure resource configurations (resource groups, RBAC, policies, Log Analytics workspace) across every new subscription created in their organization. The configuration must be version-controlled and consistent. Which service automates this subscription-level baseline deployment?
options: Azure Blueprints — define and deploy subscription-level artifacts (ARM templates.
Azure Resource Manager templates deployed manually to each new subscription
Terraform automation triggered by an Azure DevOps pipeline on subscription creation events
Azure Policy initiatives assigned at management group scope to configure resources
questions.explanation: Azure Blueprints are designed for subscription-level governance scaffolding. A blueprint definition packages: ARM templates (for resource creation), policy assignments (for governance), role assignments (for RBAC), and resource group creation — all as a single versioned artifact. When assigned to a subscription, it deploys all artifacts consistently. Blueprints track the assignment relationship, so blueprint changes can be pushed to all assigned subscriptions. Azure Policy only manages policy assignments, not resource creation. Terraform works but isn't a native Azure governance service tested on AZ-305. role assignments, policy assignments, resource groups) as a versioned, auditable package that can be assigned to subscriptions

questions.question: An architect needs to design a storage solution for a data science team. The team needs to store petabytes of raw CSV, Parquet, and JSON files in a hierarchical folder structure, with role-based access at both folder and file level. Query tools must be able to read files using standard tools. Which Azure storage service is most appropriate?
options: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2.
Azure Managed Disks with NFS v4.1 protocol for shared file system access
Azure Files (SMB) with directory-level permissions for hierarchical folder access
Azure Blob Storage (flat namespace) with container-level RBAC for access control
questions.explanation: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (ADLS Gen2) is Azure Blob Storage with hierarchical namespace (HNS) enabled. HNS provides: true directory operations (rename/delete are O(1) atomic operations, not O(n) copies), POSIX-compliant ACLs for file-and-folder-level access control (owner, group, other with rwx permissions), and 10x+ performance improvement for analytics operations. It supports Parquet/CSV/JSON natively and integrates with Azure Synapse, Databricks, and HDInsight. Flat-namespace Blob has no folder-level POSIX ACLs. Azure Files uses SMB, not optimized for analytics. built on Azure Blob with hierarchical namespace (HNS) enabled, supporting POSIX-compliant ACLs at file and directory level, optimized for analytics with massive throughput

questions.question: A solutions architect must choose a database for storing user profiles in a social media application. User profiles have variable schemas (some users have optional fields, nested arrays of interests, and linked accounts). The application expects 100,000 reads/second with consistent single-digit millisecond latency. Which database is most appropriate?
options: Azure SQL Database — use JSON columns for flexible schema support
Azure Cosmos DB with the NoSQL API.
Azure Table Storage — simple key-value store with flexible schema at lower cost
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale tier — can scale reads to 100K/s with up to 4 read replicas
questions.explanation: Variable-schema user profiles (nested arrays, optional fields, linked accounts) map naturally to a document model (JSON). Cosmos DB NoSQL API stores each user profile as a JSON document, supports nested structures natively without table joins, and scales to any throughput by provisioning Request Units (RUs) — auto-scale RU mode handles 100K reads/second without pre-provisioning. Single-digit ms P99 latency is a contractual SLA, not just a target. SQL Database JSON columns add relational overhead and don't scale horizontally. Table Storage lacks query flexibility for nested properties. schema-free, horizontally scalable to millions of RU/s, sub-10ms P99 latency globally, ideal for variable-schema documents

questions.question: An architect is designing a solution that will run thousands of short-lived (5-15 second) background tasks triggered by messages in an Azure Storage Queue. The code is simple, stateless, and must scale to zero when the queue is empty to minimize costs. What is the most cost-effective compute option?
options: Azure Functions consumption plan with Storage Queue trigger.
Azure Kubernetes Service with KEDA queue-based autoscaling
Azure Container Apps with Storage Queue KEDA scaler
Azure Logic Apps consumption plan triggered by Storage Queue
questions.explanation: Azure Functions consumption plan is purpose-built for this pattern: event-triggered, short-lived, stateless tasks. The Storage Queue trigger uses KEDA internally to scale from 0 to N instances based on queue depth (up to 200 concurrent function instances per plan). Billing is per 100ms execution units — with 5-15 second tasks, this is highly cost-effective. The first 1M executions per month are free. Scale-to-zero means no cost when the queue is empty. AKS and Container Apps add management overhead. Logic Apps are designed for workflow orchestration, not high-throughput message processing. scales automatically from 0 to hundreds of instances based on queue depth, billing is per execution (first 1M free/month)

questions.question: A company uses Azure DevOps pipelines to deploy infrastructure and applications. The pipelines require access to Azure Key Vault secrets (API keys, certificates) during deployment. The best practice is to avoid storing secrets in pipeline variables or service connection credentials. How should the pipeline access secrets securely?
options: Store secrets in Azure App Configuration and reference them in the pipeline via environment variables
Store secrets as encrypted Azure DevOps variable group secrets linked directly to a Key Vault.
Pass secrets as base64-encoded parameters in pipeline triggers from a secure webhook
Hardcode secrets in pipeline YAML files and use Azure Repos access controls to restrict who can view the file
questions.explanation: Azure DevOps Variable Groups support direct Key Vault integration: the variable group is linked to a Key Vault and a service principal, and specified secrets are fetched directly from Key Vault at pipeline run time — they are never stored in Azure DevOps. Pipeline tasks use the variable group secrets as masked pipeline variables. The service principal used for Key Vault access needs Key Vault Secrets Get permissions. This pattern keeps secrets centralized in Key Vault with rotation, auditing, and access control managed there. the variable group syncs values from Key Vault at pipeline run time using a service principal

questions.question: An architect is designing a solution to process files uploaded to Azure Blob Storage — each new file must trigger an image resizing function within 30 seconds. The system processes 10,000 file uploads per hour. Which trigger type provides the most reliable near-real-time processing?
options: Azure Functions with a Timer trigger running every 30 seconds to check for new blobs
Azure Functions triggered by Event Grid (Blob Created event from Storage).
Azure Logic Apps with a Recurrence trigger checking for new blobs every minute
Azure Functions with an Azure Blob Storage trigger — polls the container for new blobs on a schedule
questions.explanation: Azure Blob Storage Trigger (native) uses polling, which can have 10-minute delays for large containers. The recommended pattern for near-real-time processing is using Azure Event Grid: Storage Blob Created events are delivered within milliseconds, and Event Grid triggers a Function directly. At 10,000 uploads/hour (~2.7/second), Event Grid handles this comfortably. The Event Grid subscription filters for blob.created events and routes them to the Function endpoint. This is the AZ-305-recommended pattern for event-driven blob processing. event-driven, sub-30-second delivery, no polling overhead at 10K uploads/hour

questions.question: A company needs to deploy an application across multiple Azure regions for global availability. The application uses Azure Service Bus for messaging. The messaging layer must continue to work if an entire Azure region becomes unavailable. What feature provides this for Service Bus?
options: Azure Service Bus Federation for active-active message replication across regions using Azure Functions
Service Bus Premium with availability zones — protects against datacenter failures within a region
Azure Traffic Manager DNS routing across two separate Service Bus namespaces in different regions
Service Bus Geo-Disaster Recovery (Geo-DR).
questions.explanation: Service Bus Geo-Disaster Recovery pairs a primary namespace with a secondary namespace in a different region. It synchronizes entity metadata (queues, topics, subscriptions) but NOT message data — messages in flight are not replicated. On failover, the secondary becomes the new primary and the same alias connection string resolves to the secondary. Applications reconnect automatically via the alias. Availability Zones (option C) protect against datacenter failures within a region, not full regional outages. Federation (option D) does replicate messages but is more complex. creates a paired namespace in a secondary region with metadata synchronization; on failover, the secondary becomes primary with a new connection string

questions.question: A company's compliance team requires that ALL changes to Azure resources (creates, updates, deletes) in their production subscription be logged and retained for 1 year. The logs must be queryable. What is the correct configuration?
options: Configure a Diagnostic Setting at the subscription level to export Activity Logs to a Log Analytics workspace with 1-year retention.
Deploy Microsoft Sentinel and connect the Azure Activity data connector — Sentinel provides 1-year retention by default
Enable Azure Policy with the 'Audit if Activity Log is not retained' built-in initiative
Enable Azure Security Center (Defender for Cloud) on the subscription — it logs all resource changes automatically
questions.explanation: Azure Activity Logs capture all control-plane operations (resource creates, updates, deletes, RBAC changes, policy assignments) for the subscription. By default they're retained 90 days. To retain for 1 year: create a Diagnostic Setting at the subscription scope to export Activity Logs to a Log Analytics workspace (configure 365-day retention) or Azure Storage. The workspace enables KQL querying. This is standard configuration — no additional services like Defender or Sentinel are required, though they may augment it. or to Azure Storage for longer retention

questions.question: An architect needs to design a solution where an Azure Function needs to call multiple Azure services (Blob Storage, Cosmos DB, Key Vault) without storing any credentials or connection strings in the function's application settings. Which identity pattern is recommended?
options: Store encrypted credentials in Azure Key Vault and configure the Function to fetch them using the Key Vault reference syntax in App Settings

Use system-assigned Managed Identity for the Azure Function and grant the identity appropriate RBAC roles on each target service (Storage Blob Data Contributor, Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor, Key Vault Secrets User)
Create a service principal in Azure AD with certificates stored in Key Vault for authentication
Store all connection strings in Azure App Configuration with access key authentication
questions.explanation: Managed Identity eliminates credential management entirely — there are no secrets to store, rotate, or secure. The system-assigned MI is automatically created and bound to the Function lifecycle. Azure services that support Azure AD authentication (Blob Storage, Cosmos DB, Key Vault, Service Bus, Event Hubs, SQL Database) can authenticate the managed identity via RBAC or access policies. This is the #1 AZ-305 recommended pattern for Azure-to-Azure service authentication. Key Vault references (option D) still require an authentication credential for Key Vault itself.

questions.question: A company wants to build a serverless event-driven architecture where order placement events trigger inventory updates, billing, and notification workflows independently. If one downstream service is temporarily unavailable, the event must be retried without losing it. Which Azure messaging service is designed for this pattern?
options: Azure Event Grid — serverless event routing with at-least-once delivery and configurable retry policies;.
Azure Storage Queue — simple queuing with at-least-once delivery for background job processing
Azure Service Bus — reliable message queuing with competing consumers for ordered processing
Azure Event Hubs — high-throughput streaming for real-time analytics on order events
questions.explanation: Azure Event Grid is purpose-built for event-driven pub/sub scenarios: publishers emit events (Order Placed), and multiple subscribers (inventory service, billing service, notification service) receive independent copies. Event Grid provides at-least-once delivery with built-in retry (exponential backoff, up to 24 hours), dead-lettering for undeliverable events, and subscriber isolation (one subscriber's failure doesn't affect others). Service Bus is for reliable ordered queue-based messaging (point-to-point or pub/sub with sessions). Event Hubs is for high-throughput telemetry streaming with consumer groups. each subscriber (inventory, billing, notification) receives the event independently and retries on failure

questions.question: A company needs to deploy a highly available web application in Azure with connection-based session affinity (sticky sessions) and SSL offloading. The web tier has 10 VMs in the same VNet. Which load balancer supports these requirements?
options: Azure Front Door — global application delivery with SSL offloading and session affinity at the edge
Azure Traffic Manager — DNS-based load balancer with session affinity for global deployments
Azure Load Balancer Standard — provides layer 4 load balancing with health probes but no session affinity or SSL termination
Azure Application Gateway.
questions.explanation: Azure Application Gateway is a layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) load balancer. Key features for this scenario: Cookie-based affinity inserts a custom cookie on the first response, binding the client to a specific backend for subsequent requests (sticky sessions). SSL/TLS offloading terminates HTTPS at the gateway, allowing HTTP communication to backends (reducing backend CPU load). WAF can be added for web application protection. ALB Standard is layer 4 — it can do hash-based affinity (source IP) but not cookie-based, and doesn't terminate SSL. Traffic Manager is DNS-level (no sticky sessions within a region). layer 7 load balancer with cookie-based session affinity (sticky sessions), SSL/TLS offloading, WAF integration, and URL-based routing

questions.question: An architect needs to design an Azure solution for running a legacy application that requires a Windows Server 2012 R2 environment. The company policy mandates that all Azure VMs must use the latest security updates. How should the patching strategy be designed?
options: Manual patching by system administrators via RDP on each VM monthly
Azure Update Manager (formerly Update Management Center).
Azure Automation Hybrid Runbook Worker for running patch scripts on VMs
Azure Guest OS automatic patching enabled — Azure automatically applies all patches without scheduling
questions.explanation: Azure Update Manager provides centralized patch management for Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers. It: assesses missing patches in real-time without deploying a management solution, creates patching schedules with maintenance windows to minimize disruption, supports reboot preferences, pre/post maintenance scripts, and cross-subscription multi-VM management from a single view. It supports Windows Server 2012 R2 through current versions. Guest OS automatic patching (option D) is limited to Azure-recommended patches and has limited schedule control — not suitable for controlled production environments. centrally assesses patch compliance and orchestrates patching schedules across Azure VMs including legacy OS versions, with maintenance windows and pre/post scripts

questions.question: A company needs a storage solution for SMB file shares that Windows VMs access like traditional on-premises network drives. The solution must support Active Directory authentication for access control and provide 99.99% availability SLA. Which Azure service provides this?
options: Azure NetApp Files for enterprise NFS and SMB workloads
Azure Disk Storage with shared disk configuration for clustered file server
Azure Files Premium with SMB 3.0 protocol.
Azure Blob Storage with NFS v3 protocol for Windows VM access
questions.explanation: Azure Files provides fully managed SMB file shares in Azure. Premium tier with ZRS (Zone-Redundant Storage) provides 99.99% SLA. Azure AD Kerberos authentication (or on-premises AD DS integration) allows existing AD users/groups to access shares with their domain credentials — no separate user management. Windows VMs mount the share as a network drive using standard UNC paths. This is the recommended migration target for on-premises file servers. NetApp Files is for high-performance NFS/SMB but at significantly higher cost. Blob NFS is for Linux POSIX workloads. Azure AD Kerberos authentication for hybrid AD environments, and ZRS (Zone-Redundant Storage) for 99.99% availability SLA

questions.question: A solutions architect needs to design a globally distributed application that caches frequently read data to minimize database load. The cache must be highly available within a region and should share no single point of failure between cache and primary database. Which Azure caching solution supports replication within a region for HA?
options: Azure Cosmos DB integrated cache for sub-millisecond reads
Azure Content Delivery Network (CDN) for caching API responses at edge locations globally
Azure Table Storage with caching enabled for frequently accessed rows
Azure Cache for Redis Standard or Premium tier.
questions.explanation: Azure Cache for Redis is the managed in-memory data store for caching, session storage, and message brokering. Standard tier provides a two-node primary-replica setup with automatic failover and 99.9% SLA. Premium tier adds clustering (multiple shards), persistence (RDB/AOF), and geo-replication for cross-region cache reads. This directly addresses the HA requirement within a region. CDN caches static content at edge, not application-layer cache. Table Storage is a persistent database, not a cache. Cosmos DB integrated cache is a feature for Cosmos DB itself, not a general-purpose caching layer. supports primary-replica replication within a region, 99.9% SLA (Standard) or 99.95% (Premium), automatic failover, geo-replication (Premium) for cross-region scenarios

questions.question: An architect is designing a network solution that requires Azure VMs in one VNet to communicate with services in a third-party SaaS provider's Azure VNet, without exposing traffic to the internet and without requiring VNet peering. What technology enables this?
options: Use Azure ExpressRoute Microsoft Peering to route traffic between both VNets through the Azure backbone
Deploy a Site-to-Site VPN between the company's VNet and the SaaS provider's VNet
Configure VNet peering between the company's VNet and the SaaS provider's VNet
The SaaS provider exposes their service via Azure Private Link as a Private Endpoint in the consumer's VNet.
questions.explanation: Azure Private Link enables service providers to expose their services as Private Link Services. Consumers create a Private Endpoint in their own VNet, which receives a private IP in the consumer's address space. Traffic flows from the consumer VM → consumer VNet → Azure backbone → Private Link Service → provider VNet without VNet peering (no overlapping IP concerns), without internet exposure, and without the provider needing visibility into the consumer's network. This is the standard pattern for SaaS providers (including Microsoft PaaS services) and enterprise service sharing. the consumer connects using a private IP within their own VNet without VNet peering

questions.question: An organization needs to implement an Azure governance model that assigns specific subscription management responsibilities to different teams: a Networking team that manages all virtual networks across subscriptions, a Security team that manages Azure Policy, and individual app teams that manage their own resource groups. What RBAC design achieves this?
options: Grant all teams Owner access at the root management group level for maximum flexibility
Networking team: Network Contributor role at root/networking management group;.
Create a single shared service account with Owner access and share credentials between teams
Grant all teams Contributor at subscription level and use Azure Policy to restrict what each team can do
questions.explanation: AZ-305 governance best practice: assign RBAC at the lowest scope that meets requirements. Network Contributor at MG/subscription scope gives the networking team management rights over VNets without access to other resources. Policy Contributor at MG scope allows the security team to create/assign policies without infrastructure access. App team Contributor at resource group scope gives full resource management rights within their boundary without cross-team access. This implements separation of duties — each team has rights over their domain only. Owner at root MG is a massive security risk. Security team: Policy Contributor at root MG; App teams: Contributor role scoped to their resource groups — each team has only the permissions needed at the appropriate scope

questions.question: A company is designing a solution for sharing large datasets between Azure Data Factory pipelines and Azure Machine Learning workspaces. The datasets are stored in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2. Both services need read/write access without using storage account keys. What is the recommended identity pattern?
options: Enable system-assigned managed identities for both ADF and AML.
Create a shared storage account key and store it in Azure Key Vault, referenced by both services
Use Azure AD service principals with certificates stored in Key Vault for both services
Configure SAS tokens with read/write permissions for both ADF and AML with 30-day expiry
questions.explanation: Managed Identities for Azure services (ADF, AML, AKS, Functions, etc.) eliminate the need for credentials entirely. Both Azure Data Factory and Azure Machine Learning support system-assigned managed identities. Granting each identity the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on the ADLS Gen2 account allows read/write access using Azure AD token authentication. No keys, no SAS tokens, no certificates — no credential rotation needed. The identities are tied to the service lifecycle. This is the recommended pattern for service-to-service authentication in Azure. grant each the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on the ADLS Gen2 account — no credentials needed

questions.question: A company is planning to move workloads to Azure but must maintain compliance with data residency requirements — all data must remain within the European Union (EU). How should the architect enforce this at scale across 20 subscriptions?
options: Use Azure Cost Management budget alerts to notify when resources are deployed outside EU regions
Apply an Azure Policy initiative at the management group level with 'Allowed locations' set to 'West Europe' and 'North Europe',.
Configure Azure Blueprints to deploy resource group locks in EU regions only
Instruct developers to always select EU regions when deploying resources — rely on training and process
questions.explanation: Data residency enforcement requires a preventive technical control, not a process or detective control. Azure Policy 'Allowed locations' with Deny effect at management group scope blocks resource deployment to any non-EU region across ALL 20 subscriptions automatically. The 'Allowed locations for resource groups' companion policy ensures resource groups themselves can only be created in EU regions (resource groups have a location metadata that determines where group-level metadata is stored). Policy at MG scope covers current and future subscriptions, satisfying the at-scale requirement. and 'Allowed locations for resource groups' policy for resource group creation — Deny effect prevents any non-EU deployments

questions.question: An architect must design a solution for an application that requires 500 GB of NVMe SSD storage with consistent sub-millisecond I/O latency for a high-performance SQL workload. The storage must be available only to the specific VM running the SQL workload. Which Azure storage type is appropriate?
options: Azure Managed Disk Premium SSD (P50-P80) — well-proven performance with consistent P99 latency
Azure Premium SSD v2 — provides higher IOPS than Premium SSD with configurable performance at granular settings
Azure Ultra Disk — provides configurable IOPS (up to 160,000 per disk).
Azure Files Premium tier with SMB for SQL Server data files
questions.explanation: Azure Ultra Disk provides the highest performance tier for Azure managed disks: sub-millisecond I/O latency consistently at P99, up to 160,000 IOPS and 4,000 MB/s throughput per disk, and configurable IOPS/throughput independently of disk size (you can have a 500 GB disk with maximum IOPS). Ultra Disk is exclusively attached to one VM (no shared disk by default). It requires availability zone support and supported VM sizes. Premium SSD v2 also provides high configurable performance but Ultra Disk delivers the lowest guaranteed latency for demanding SQL workloads. Azure Files SMB adds network latency, unsuitable for SQL data files. throughput, and disk size with sub-millisecond latency, attached exclusively to a single VM via managed disk

questions.question: You must design storage for a workload writing 5 GB log files every minute. The data is read once for analytics within 24 hours, then never touched again but must be retained for 7 years for compliance. Which TWO design choices fit BEST?
options: Write logs to the Hot access tier in ADLS Gen2
Apply a lifecycle policy that moves blobs to Archive after 1 day
Use Premium block blob storage for the entire 7-year retention
Write logs directly to Archive tier and rehydrate them for analytics
questions.explanation: Hot tier is appropriate for the freshly-written data being read within 24h. A lifecycle policy that transitions to Archive after 1 day matches the access pattern (cold for 7 years). Premium is overkill and expensive for cold logs. Writing to Archive directly is impossible — Archive is offline; reading requires rehydration which takes hours.
